title: Volim burek
reviewerNotes: Full draft to Lesson 1 exemplar bar. ready for human review before publish.
storyBeat: Ana’s food disasters begin with burek. Emir teaches likes and a gentle accusative chunk.

vocabulary: Name burek, sirnica, zeljanica, hljeb, and jogurt
Use volim and ne volim for likes and dislikes
Say gladan or gladna, ukusno, and dobar tek
grammar: Use Volim plus a food object as one ready chunk
Use Ne volim for a polite dislike
Match gladan and gladna to the speaker
culture: In BiH, burek means meat, and cheese pie is sirnica
See Livno highland cheese beyond the café street

grammar.title: Volim + object
grammar.explanation: Volim means I love or I like. Put the food after it as a ready chunk. Say Volim burek. Say Volim kahvu. For many feminine food nouns ending in -a, the spoken object often ends in -u. Say Volim sirnicu. Say Volim zeljanicu. Learn the pairs as phrases first. Do not memorize a full case table in this lesson.

grammar.title: Ne volim
grammar.explanation: Add ne before volim to say you do not like something. Say Ne volim luk. Say Ne volim čaj. Keep it soft and clear. You can still be polite while you refuse a filling.

grammar.title: Gladan / gladna
grammar.explanation: Match the adjective to who is speaking. Emir says Ja sam gladan. Ana says Ja sam gladna. Then order food and finish with Dobar tek!

culture.title: Burek is meat, and Livno sends cheese
culture.body: On a Bosnian street, burek means a meat pita. If you want cheese, you ask for sirnica. If you want spinach or greens, you ask for zeljanica. Emir takes Ana to a buregdžinica and then shows her a postcard from Livno in western Bosnia. The card shows highland pastures that are famous for Livanjski sir. The café can stay their home base, but today’s food map also points west to Livno cheese country. Ana practices saying what she loves before her first bite turns into a flaky little disaster.

lessonBlocks.title: Lesson A: Food words on the tray
lessonBlocks.body: Start with the classics on the tray. Burek is the meat pastry. Sirnica is the cheese pita. Zeljanica is the greens pita. Pita is the general word for a phyllo pie. Add hljeb, jogurt, meso, sir, voće, and povrće next. Say each word twice. Mark the BiH spelling of hljeb with lj. Emir points at the tray and refuses the tourist trap sentence burek sa sirom. In Bosnian that fight is real. Burek comes with meat.
tips: Burek is meat. Sirnica is cheese. Zeljanica is greens.
Type hljeb with lj, not a soft English h-leb guess

lessonBlocks.title: Lesson B: Volim / ne volim at the counter
lessonBlocks.body: Build your counter phrases as full sentences. Say Volim burek. Say Volim sirnicu. Say Ne volim luk. Ana says Ja sam gladna. Emir says Ja sam gladan. Finish with Ukusno! and Dobar tek! Ana tries a too-hot bite, drops flakes on Mrvica, and still finishes the sentence. Food disasters are allowed. Silent pointing is not the goal.
tips: Keep the chunks Volim, Ne volim, and Dobar tek ready
Use gladna if you are Ana. Use gladan if you are Emir.

funFacts.title: No cheese in the word burek
funFacts.body: In Bosnia and Herzegovina, burek means a meat pita. Tourists often ask for burek sa sirom and reveal that they learned a different regional habit. Locals treat cheese pie as sirnica instead. If you want to sound local in this lesson, keep burek for meat and sirnica for cheese.

funFacts.title: Livanjski sir
funFacts.body: Livno is famous for highland cheese, not only for mountain views. Livanjski sir comes from western Bosnia pastures with a long dairy tradition. Emir’s postcard uses that fame to pull Ana’s food map outside one city street. When you learn food words today, remember that BiH dairy pride has regional addresses.

funFacts.title: Jogurt is a partner
funFacts.body: Warm burek often arrives with jogurt on purpose. The cool yogurt balances the hot pastry and slows the first bite. People treat the pair as a small everyday ritual, not a random side. If you order burek, expect jogurt to feel like part of the meal.

funFacts.title: Mrvica tax
funFacts.body: Any flaky pita near Mrvica becomes a shared meal. Crumbs fall, the cat arrives, and ownership of the snack gets renegotiated immediately. Ana learns food words while losing pastry in real time. In this course, feeding the café cat is unofficial vocabulary practice.

civicContext.title: Local food culture, imported staples
civicContext.body: Bosnia and Herzegovina’s food culture is local, but many grocery staples still come from abroad. After the war, fragmented farmland and weak agricultural investment slowed the recovery of domestic production. Bakeries and shops often stock flour, oil, dairy, and other basics from imports even while street pita culture thrives. Loving burek is part of daily life, and that daily life still depends on a supply chain that is only partly grown at home.
